outline_action: Extract the GC-MS parameters and healthy control serum ranges for SCFAs to address the SCFA portion of the gap. Search specifically for LC-MS/MS or GC-MS protocols for inosine quantification in human serum or tumor tissue. Look for consensus guidelines or methodological papers that report SCFA or inosine concentrations specifically in cancer patient cohorts to address the cancer-specific reference range requirement.
remaining_gap: No protocol or reference ranges are provided for inosine quantification. The study does not cover human tumor tissue samples (only mouse cecum tissue and human biofluids). Reference ranges are limited to healthy controls; no cancer-specific reference ranges or consensus statements for cancer patients are identified. The method uses GC-MS, while the gap also inquires about LC-MS/MS parameters.
useful_material: This study provides a validated GC-MS protocol for quantifying short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in human serum and plasma, including specific analytical parameters (DB-FFAP column, SIM mode ions, temperature program), sample processing standards (acidification with HCl, MTBE liquid-liquid extraction, storage at −80 °C), and reference concentration ranges for acetic, propionic, butyric, and valeric acid in healthy human controls (e.g., serum acetic acid 4788–8823 ng/mL). The authors also detail a surrogate matrix approach using distilled water for calibration, validated for parallelism and matrix effects in serum.

This study provides a detailed Basic Protocol for quantifying 14 short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in human serum using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS). It specifies analytical platform parameters including the use of an Agilent 7820A GC-5977B MSD system, an HP-5 ms capillary column (30 m x 250 μm x 0.25 μm), oven temperature programming (60 °C to 325 °C), and electron impact ionization at -70 eV. The authors describe sample processing standards involving alkaline extraction (0.1 M NaOH for serum), methanol precipitation, vacuum concentration, and derivatization with N-tert-butyldimethylsilyl-N-methyltrifluoroacetamide (MTBSTFA) at 60 °C. The protocol includes storage recommendations (−80 °C for long-term) and cites the Human Metabolomics Database (HMDB) for normal concentration ranges of acetic acid in human blood (26.8 to 64.2 μM) as a reference for healthy controls.

This study confirms the application of liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) for quantifying serum inosine and short-chain fatty acids (acetate, butyrate, isovalerate) in patients with relapsed/refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (R/R-DLBCL). The authors report associations between pretreatment serum inosine levels and progression-free survival, as well as correlations between serum fatty acid profiles and immune-related adverse events. The discussion notes that in vitro experimental concentrations of inosine (10-30 mM) exceed physiological serum levels, highlighting the distinction between experimental dosing and endogenous concentrations.
